bib.title: Big Entropy and the Generalized Linear Model (Statistical Rethinking, ch. 9)
bib.venue: Statistical Rethinking, first edition, CRC Press (book chapter, pp. 267-289)

question: How should likelihoods and priors be chosen beyond Gaussian convention, and how do link functions let linear models attach to non-Gaussian outcome distributions?
hypothesis: Betting on the maximum entropy distribution consistent with the constraints on an outcome is the most conservative choice, and generalizes regression to GLMs.
contributions: Maximum entropy as counting arrangements (pebbles, Wallis derivation)
Max entropy derivations of Gaussian and binomial
GLM recipe: max entropy likelihood plus link function (logit, log)
Warning that information criteria cannot compare different likelihood families

results.claim: With 10 pebbles in 5 buckets, the flat distribution (2 per bucket) can be realised 113400 ways, more than any other.
results.setup: 10 numbered pebbles tossed uniformly into 5 buckets; distributions A to E (Fig 9.1)
results.quote: there are 113400 ways to realize this distribution

results.claim: Information entropy of the five pebble distributions rises with the number of ways; the flat one is largest at 1.6094379 (=log 5).
results.baseline_value: 0.0000000 for all pebbles in one bucket
results.setup: Code 9.3 on p_norm of A..E (counts 0,0,10,0,0 to 2,2,2,2,2)

results.claim: Entropy is an approximation of log ways per pebble (log(ways)/10), already very good for 10 pebbles.
Among generalized normal distributions with equal variance, entropy peaks at shape beta = 2, the Gaussian.
results.setup: Generalized normal, variance 1, beta varied 1 to 4 (Fig 9.2)
results.quote: The generalized normal is perfectly Gaussian where β = 2, and that’s exactly where entropy is maximized.

results.claim: Four candidate distributions over two-draw marble sequences, all with expected value 1, have entropies 1.386294, 1.329661, 1.329661, 1.213008; the flat binomial (p=0.5) is largest.
The binomial with p=0.7 over two draws is (0.09,0.21,0.21,0.49) with entropy 1.221729.
results.setup: Expected value 1.4 blue marbles in 2 draws (code 9.7-9.8)

results.claim: Of 100000 random distributions with expected value 1.4, the largest entropy found is 1.221728, matching the binomial.
Gaussian has the highest entropy of any continuous distribution on the real line with a given variance (proof via KL divergence).
results.setup: Variance sigma^2 fixed, support minus to plus infinity
results.quote: The Gaussian has the highest entropy possible for any continuous distribution with variance σ2.

results.claim: The binomial is the maximum entropy distribution for two unordered outcomes with constant expected value.
results.setup: Constraints: two unordered events, constant expected value
results.quote: then the distribution that is most conservative is the binomial.

results.claim: Information criteria such as WAIC cannot be used to compare models with different outcome distributions, because deviance includes normalizing constants.
results.quote: Really all you have to remember is to only compare models that all use the same type of likelihood.

results.claim: No GLM coefficient gives a constant change on the outcome scale; a large beta need not mean a large effect.
results.quote: a big beta-coefficient may not correspond to a big effect on the outcome.

results.claim: With a logit link, a half-unit increase in x from log-odds 0 raises probability by about 0.25, with diminishing returns after.
results.quote: A half- unit increase in x results in about a 0.25 increase in probability.

results.claim: Poisson is the binomial limit for large n and small p with rate lambda = np; same max entropy constraints.
results.quote: a binomial distribution converges to a Poisson distribution with an expected rate of events per unit time of λ = np

limits: Chapter is conceptual, not practical; computing GLMs is deferred to chapters 10 and 11 (p.289).
Derivations are graphical and not mathematically rigorous (p.271).
Max entropy gives no guarantee of the best distribution for the real problem (p.279).
Log link extrapolates exponentially and cannot hold outside the data range (p.287).
Max entropy priors are described but not used in the book (p.289).
practices: Choose the likelihood by the constraints on the outcome and pick the maximum entropy distribution (p.267, 9.2).
Use a Gaussian likelihood only for a continuous outcome far from any bound; use binomial for counts from n trials, Poisson for counts far from a maximum (p.280-283).
Attach a logit link to a probability parameter and a log link to a positive parameter such as sigma (p.284-286).
Do not pick a likelihood by inspecting the outcome histogram (Histomancy); the Gaussian assumption concerns residuals after conditioning on predictors (p.282).
Run a sensitivity analysis on link, likelihood, linear model and priors, and report all results (p.287).
Visualize counterfactual predictions on the outcome scale because every predictor effectively interacts with itself under a link (p.286).
Compare models with WAIC/DIC/AIC only when they share the same outcome distribution type (p.288).
Use maximum entropy priors when real background information on a parameter exists; otherwise weakly informative priors are fine (p.288-289).
Check performance of any non-exponential-family likelihood like any other modeling assumption (p.284).

terms.definition: H(p) = -sum p_i log p_i, the average log-probability; the unique measure that is continuous, grows with number of events and is additive
The distribution that can happen the most ways; the most conservative distribution that obeys its constraints
A model that replaces a parameter of a likelihood function with a linear model; any likelihood can be used
A function f mapping the linear space of alpha + beta x onto the non-linear space of a parameter, preventing negative distances or probabilities above 1
logit(p) = log(p/(1-p)), the log-odds; inverse is the logistic
Maps a positive parameter to a linear model; inverse is exponentiation
Common distributions in statistical modeling, each a maximum entropy distribution for some set of constraints
Observations are independent after accounting for differences in predictors through the model
W = N!/(n1!...nm!), the number of ways a set of counts can be realized
Exploring how changes in assumptions influence inference, describing all analyses tried
